before: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) graphs provide a natural source of molecular context for missense variant pathogenicity prediction. Clarifying when PPI context adds information helps distinguish biological network signal from representation smoothing, split-dependent connectivity and complementarity to existing variant-effect scores. Interpreting performance gains from propagating protein embeddings over a shared graph requires separating protein-topology alignment, train-test connectivity, homology-related split structure and complementarity to existing variant-effect predictors. We audit these possibilities using a reconstructed ClinVar-STRING dataset of 177,213 filtered, non-conflicting ClinVar missense variants mapped to 14,123 labelled STRING proteins within a 19,622-node STRING protein-association graph used as PPI context. ESM protein language model embeddings are compared with fixed two-hop PPI-GCN propagation, CADD, AlphaMissense and fusion models using validation-selected downstream MLP classifiers. Across three classifier seeds, PPI-GCN increased mean AUC from 0.7835 to 0.7950 and mean AUPRC from 0.6116 to 0.6484. In a retained reference run used for paired graph-ablation analyses, removing direct train-test PPI edges nearly eliminated the AUC gain, protein-clustered bootstrap widened uncertainty across zero, and topology permutation returned performance close to the raw ESM range. Graph fusion also improved \CADDAM{} under the original split. Raw-ESM, edge-ablated and topology-permuted protein representations retained much of this gain, leaving limited topology-specific added value in the strong-predictor fusion setting. In the homology-aware stress test, the retained graph-fusion estimate was lower than the repeated-run architecture-matched \CADDAM{} baseline. Topology-stratified and sample-level transition analyses suggested that graph-associated gains and prediction changes were concentrated in specific network roles and error types. PPI graph augmentation acted as a context-dependent source of network information, with added value shaped by graph connectivity, split design and baseline predictor strength.
after: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) graphs can add molecular context to missense variant prediction, but their contribution depends on evaluation design and baseline strength. We audit fixed two-hop propagation of ESM protein embeddings using 177,213 ClinVar variants and a STRING association graph. Only downstream classifiers are trained. Across three seeds, propagation increased mean AUC from 0.7835 to 0.7950; protein-clustered intervals for the reference-model gains included zero. Connectivity and topology controls showed performance sensitivity, although their propagation and training settings were not fully matched. With CADD and AlphaMissense included, protein-representation controls retained much of the fusion gain. Under homology-aware splitting, the single graph-fusion estimate was below the repeated strong-predictor baseline. Topology groups and error transitions showed exploratory associations rather than established correction mechanisms. BioGRID second-network validation did not establish a consistent added benefit over raw-embedding controls. These findings support context-dependent protein-representation complementarity and careful evaluation of network-specific increments. They concern fixed propagation and should not be generalized to trained graph neural networks.

\subsection{Second-network validation}

BioGRID 5.0.262 human physical interactions \cite{Stark2006BioGRID} were mapped to the same 19,622 nodes, yielding 931,458 undirected edges after excluding RNA-related methods and ambiguous mappings. Nine classifiers covered representations under the original split and score fusion under both splits. Within this comparison, BioGRID and STRING used the same full-graph propagation convention; all models shared seeds 42--44, validation selection and a 50-epoch budget with patience five. Predictions were aligned by variant and protein identifiers and averaged in float64. Paired protein-bootstrap 95\% intervals used 2,000 resamples conditional on fitted models, without retraining or multiplicity adjustment (Supplementary Methods 5 and Table 9).
